text:
Recent work supports testing multiple intent representations, though it does not establish gains on this benchmark. [FAME (WSDM 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01457) predicts separately from final attention-head subspaces, gates their predictions, and uses per-head experts with learned routing to separate preferences. This offers a practical SASRec extension using interaction histories alone. [ICSRec (WSDM 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3616855.3635773) instead learns intents through cross-subsequence contrastive supervision: subsequences sharing a training target are treated as potential expressions of the same intent, avoiding explicit intent labels.

Temporal routing offers an alternative to simply increasing recency weights. [HM4SR (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14269) introduces timestamp embeddings into a temporal MoE, alongside multimodal experts and auxiliary objectives; its complete setup requires information beyond this task’s available inputs. [Mixture of Sequence (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20858) describes recurring interests across separated sessions, routing coherent subsequences by latent theme and combining global, short-term, and theme-specific experts. Its evidence concerns long-sequence recommendation, so transfer to sparse histories remains uncertain.

Complementarity needs separate evidence: multiple interests alone do not identify complementary purchases. A [2024 Amazon Grocery study](https://xbzrb.hbu.edu.cn/EN/10.3969/j.issn.1000-1565.2024.05.012) explicitly combines complementary/substitute relationships with purchase sequences, but does not establish applicability to these four categories. Practical inference: compare a small gated multi-interest SASRec against the baseline, then add timestamp-conditioned routing separately. Preserve an unrestricted history branch; assess gains by category and history length. Treat inferred intents and complementary relations as latent hypotheses, not observed user traits.
